q: In an LBO sources and uses table, total sources must equal what?
explain: The sources and uses table must balance: the funding raised (sources) equals the capital required (uses), similar to the balance sheet equation.
hook: Every dollar spent needs a dollar raised.

sources.title: Basics of an LBO Model | Training Tutorial
sources.quote: In the sources and uses of funds table, the total sources must equate to the total uses (Total Uses = Total Sources), akin to the fundamental balance sheet equation .

sources.title: LBO Model: Sources & Uses [Video Tutorial]
sources.quote: Finally, add up Total Sources at the bottom and ensure that it equals Total Uses.

q: Which line item is usually the plug that makes sources equal uses in an LBO?
explain: After the debt and other sources are set, the financial sponsor's equity contribution fills the remaining gap so that total sources equal total uses.
hook: Debt first, equity fills the gap.

sources.title: Basics of an LBO Model | Training Tutorial
sources.quote: The remaining amount for the Sources and Uses to be equal is the equity contribution by the financial sponsor (i.e. the equity investment to “plug” the remaining funds required).

sources.title: LBO Model: Sources & Uses [Video Tutorial]
sources.quote: Then, calculate Investor Equity by setting it equal to Total Uses — “Sources So Far” — all the sources of funding ABOVE the Investor Equity line item.

q: On which side of the sources and uses table do transaction fees and financing fees appear?
explain: Total uses include the purchase enterprise value plus transaction fees (advisory, legal, consulting) and financing fees (debt issuance costs).
hook: Fees are money spent, so they are uses.

sources.title: Basics of an LBO Model | Training Tutorial
sources.quote: Total Uses ➝ Purchase Enterprise Value (TEV), Transaction Fees, Financing Fees

sources.title: Sources and Uses of Funds | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: Uses → The “Uses” side calculates the total amount of capital required to make the acquisition (i.e. the purchase price and transaction fees).

q: In the LBO sources and uses table, management rollover equity is shown as a source or a use of funds?
explain: Rollover by the founder or management reduces how much the PE firm must pay, so it is treated as another source of funding.
hook: Management's rolled stake helps fund the deal.

sources.title: LBO Model: Sources & Uses [Video Tutorial]
sources.quote: Founder or Management Rollover — If the Founder or management team owns a % of the company now and wants to keep it, this also reduces the amount the PE firm pays — and therefore it’s another Source of funding and only appears under Sources.

sources.title: Management Buyout (MBO) | Transaction Structure + Examples
sources.quote: From the perspective of the financial sponsor, the rollover equity by management is a “source” of funds that reduce:

q: In a sources and uses schedule, debt that is assumed rather than refinanced appears on which side?
explain: Assumed debt simply stays on the balance sheet, so it is both a source and a use and has no impact on the cash required for the deal.

sources.title: LBO Model: Sources & Uses [Video Tutorial]
sources.quote: Debt Assumed — This appears under BOTH the Sources AND the Uses sides and has no impact on the cash required to do the deal. It simply stays on the Balance Sheet, so it’s both a Source and a Use of funds and doesn’t impact us at all.

q: When the target uses its own excess cash to help fund the buyout, is that cash a source or a use of funds?
explain: Excess cash used reduces the number of shares the PE firm must buy, and therefore the amount it must pay, so it is a source of funds.

sources.title: LBO Model: Sources & Uses [Video Tutorial]
sources.quote: Excess Cash Used — The company uses its own cash to purchase some of its shares required to complete the deal. This REDUCES the number of shares the PE firm must buy, and therefore reduces the amount the PE firm must pay, so it’s a Source of funds.

q: Which return metric accounts for the time value of money: IRR or MOIC?
explain: IRR is an annualized return that depends on the timing of cash flows, while MOIC only compares proceeds to invested capital regardless of when the exit occurs.
hook: IRR has a clock; MOIC does not.

sources.title: Multiple on Invested Capital (MOIC) | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: The fact that the MOIC metric neglects the concept of time is the reason the internal rate of return (IRR) – i.e. a returns metric that considers the duration of the holding period – must be calculated as well to generate a complete picture of investment performance, inclusive of the passage of time.

sources.title: Maximizing Returns: Understanding MOIC in Private Equity
sources.quote: While IRR considers the time value of money and the timing of cash flows, MOIC focuses exclusively on the relationship between the realized value and the initial invested capital.

q: What does the returns abbreviation MoM stand for?
explain: MoM is another name for MOIC (multiple on invested capital), also called cash-on-cash.

sources.title: Maximizing Returns: Understanding MOIC in Private Equity
sources.quote: MOIC is usually synonymous with the terms “cash-on-cash” and “multiple-on-money (MoM)”.

sources.title: Basics of an LBO Model | Training Tutorial
sources.quote: After calculating the exit equity value because of the sponsor, the key LBO return metrics – i.e. the internal rate of return (IRR) and multiple of money (MoM) – can be estimated.

q: A sponsor invests $100 million of equity and receives $300 million in total proceeds; what is the MOIC?
explain: MOIC equals total value returned divided by invested capital: $300m / $100m = 3.0x.

sources.title: Maximizing Returns: Understanding MOIC in Private Equity
sources.quote: MOIC = Total Value / Invested Capital

sources.title: Basics of an LBO Model | Training Tutorial
sources.quote: The multiple on invested capital (MOIC) is the ratio between the proceeds retrieved from an investment and the original investment.

q: Roughly what IRR does doubling your money (2.0x) over 5 years imply?
explain: A 2.0x MOIC over a 5-year hold implies an IRR of about 15%; the Rule of 72 (72 / 5 ≈ 14) gives a similar estimate.

sources.title: Multiple on Invested Capital (MOIC) | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: 2.0x MOIC in 5 Years | * ~15% IRR

sources.title: How To Quickly Calculate IRR in LBO Models [Video Tutorial]
sources.quote: Double Your Money in 5 Years = ~15% IRR

q: Roughly what IRR does doubling your money (2.0x) over 3 years imply?
explain: A 2.0x MOIC over 3 years implies roughly a 25% IRR; 100% / 3 is about 33%, and compounding brings the true rate down to about 75% of that.
hook: Double in three: a quarter a year.

sources.title: Multiple on Invested Capital (MOIC) | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: 2.0x MOIC in 3 Years | * ~25% IRR

sources.title: How To Quickly Calculate IRR in LBO Models [Video Tutorial]
sources.quote: For example, if you double your money in 3 years, 100% / 3 = 33%. 75% of 33% is about 25%, which is the approximate IRR in this case.

q: Roughly what IRR does tripling your money (3.0x) over 5 years imply?
explain: A 3.0x MOIC over a 5-year hold implies an IRR of about 25%, the same IRR as doubling money in 3 years.
hook: Triple in five equals double in three.

sources.title: Multiple on Invested Capital (MOIC) | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: 3.0x MOIC in 5 Years | * ~25% IRR

sources.title: How To Quickly Calculate IRR in LBO Models [Video Tutorial]
sources.quote: Triple Your Money in 5 Years = ~25% IRR

q: Roughly what IRR does tripling your money (3.0x) over 3 years imply?
explain: A 3.0x MOIC over 3 years implies an IRR of about 45%.

sources.title: Multiple on Invested Capital (MOIC) | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: 3.0x MOIC in 3 Years | * ~45% IRR

sources.title: How To Quickly Calculate IRR in LBO Models [Video Tutorial]
sources.quote: Triple Your Money in 3 Years = ~45% IRR

q: Which rule estimates the years needed to double an investment by dividing a number by the annual rate of return?
explain: The Rule of 72 is a back-of-the-envelope shortcut: divide 72 by the annual rate of return to estimate doubling time, which is handy for paper LBOs.

sources.title: Rule of 72 - Formula, Calculate the Time for an Investment to Double
sources.quote: The rule is a shortcut, or back-of-the-envelope, calculation to determine the amount of time for an investment to double in value. The simple calculation is dividing 72 by the annual interest rate.

sources.title: Paper LBO Tutorial | Practice Training Guide - Wall Street Prep
sources.quote: The approximate number of years necessary for the investment value to double in size can be determined by dividing 72 by the rate of return.

q: Using the Rule of 72, about how many years does it take to double an investment at a 12% annual return?
explain: 72 divided by 12 equals 6, so the investment roughly doubles in about six years.

sources.title: Rule of 72 - Formula, Calculate the Time for an Investment to Double
sources.quote: It will take approximately six years for John’s investment to double in value.

sources.title: Paper LBO Tutorial | Practice Training Guide - Wall Street Prep
sources.quote: The approximate number of years necessary for the investment value to double in size can be determined by dividing 72 by the rate of return.

q: Besides EBITDA growth and multiple expansion, what is the third classic driver of LBO returns?
explain: LBO returns come from EBITDA growth, multiple expansion, and using and repaying significant debt (or generating cash); as debt is paid down, equity value increases.
hook: Grow it, re-rate it, pay it down.

sources.title: LBO - Returns Attribution Analysis (18:42) - BIWS
sources.quote: 3. A significant amount of debt must be used and repaid and/or a significant amount of cash must be generated in the same period.

sources.title: LBO Value Creation Through Leverage & Ops | Guide | Macabacus
sources.quote: As the debt is paid down, the value of the equity increase and healthy returns are generated, as demonstrated below:

q: Multiple expansion means the exit EBITDA multiple is higher or lower than the purchase EBITDA multiple?
explain: Multiple expansion is buying at one valuation multiple and selling at a higher one (buy low, sell high).

sources.title: LBO - Returns Attribution Analysis (18:42) - BIWS
sources.quote: 2. There must be multiple expansion (exit EBITDA multiple is higher than the purchase EBITDA multiple).

sources.title: LBO Value Creation Through Leverage & Ops | Guide | Macabacus
sources.quote: In addition, expansion of market valuation multiples (i.e. buy low, sell high) can create value for the financial sponsor.

q: Which LBO value creation lever is market-driven and largely outside the control of the company and sponsor?
explain: Multiple expansion depends on market valuations, so it is unreliable and hard to predict; sponsors prefer returns from EBITDA growth and debt paydown.
hook: The market sets the multiple, not you.

sources.title: LBO Value Creation Through Leverage & Ops | Guide | Macabacus
sources.quote: Note, however, that multiple expansion is market-driven and beyond the control of the company and the sponsor.

sources.title: LBO - Returns Attribution Analysis (18:42) - BIWS
sources.quote: Ideally, we would prefer nothing from multiple expansion as it’s unreliable and hard to predict or take advantage of.

q: In returns attribution, the multiple expansion contribution equals (exit multiple minus purchase multiple) times which EBITDA figure?
explain: Multiple expansion = (Exit Multiple - Purchase Multiple) x Final Year EBITDA, capturing how much more value the final EBITDA contributes.

sources.title: LBO - Returns Attribution Analysis (18:42) - BIWS
sources.quote: (Exit Multiple – Purchase Multiple) * Final Year EBITDA

q: In returns attribution, the EBITDA growth contribution equals (final EBITDA minus initial EBITDA) times which multiple?
explain: EBITDA growth = (Final Year EBITDA - Initial EBITDA) x EBITDA Purchase Multiple; debt paydown and cash generation is backed into as the remainder.
hook: Growth at entry price; re-rating on exit EBITDA.

sources.title: LBO - Returns Attribution Analysis (18:42) - BIWS
sources.quote: (Final Year EBITDA – Initial EBITDA) * EBITDA Purchase Multiple

q: All else equal, does a smaller upfront sponsor equity contribution raise or lower LBO returns?
explain: Returns are a direct function of the equity required: the less equity the PE firm contributes, the higher the returns to the fund (and vice versa).

sources.title: Sources and Uses of Funds | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: All else being equal, the less equity contributed by the PE firm, the higher the returns to the fund (and vice versa).

sources.title: Basics of an LBO Model | Training Tutorial
sources.quote: All else being equal, the lower the required upfront equity contribution from the financial sponsor, the higher the returns.

q: In a dividend recapitalization, what funds the special dividend paid to the sponsor?
explain: The portfolio company raises additional debt and uses the proceeds to pay a special one-time dividend; the dividends come from new debt, not the company's earnings.

sources.title: Dividend Recapitalization (Recap) | LBO Transaction
sources.quote: In a dividend recapitalization transaction, often abbreviated as “dividend recap”, the post-LBO portfolio company of a financial sponsor raises more debt capital to issue its equity shareholders (i.e. the private equity firm) a special, one-time cash dividend.

sources.title: Dividend Recapitalization - Definition, Risks, Example
sources.quote: The source of the dividends distributed as a result of dividend recapitalization is newly incurred debt, not the company’s earnings.

q: What effect does a dividend recap typically have on the fund's IRR?
explain: Because the sponsor receives proceeds earlier, a dividend recap raises IRR; it is a way to monetize the investment before a full exit.

sources.title: Dividend Recapitalization (Recap) | LBO Transaction
sources.quote: In particular, a dividend recap can positively impact the fund’s internal rate of return (IRR) , since the IRR is positively affected by the earlier monetization and distribution of funds.

sources.title: Returns Attribution Analysis | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: Dividend recaps are performed to monetize profits from the LBO prior to a complete exit, and the timing of the recap has the additional benefit of increasing the fund’s IRR since the proceeds are received earlier.

q: What happens to the portfolio company's leverage after a dividend recap?
explain: A dividend recap adds new debt to fund the payout, so leverage rises along with the probability of default.

sources.title: Dividend Recapitalization - Definition, Risks, Example
sources.quote: The recapitalization directly impacts the company’s capital structure since its leverage increases.

sources.title: Dividend Recapitalization (Recap) | LBO Transaction
sources.quote: When a private equity firm completes a dividend recapitalization , additional debt financing is raised with the specific intent to issue a special, one-time dividend using the cash proceeds from the newly-raised debt.

q: What is the term for sale proceeds that a seller reinvests into the equity of the post-acquisition company?
explain: Rollover equity lets the seller (often management) keep a stake in the new entity, aligning incentives and signaling belief in further upside.
hook: Roll your chips into the next hand.

sources.title: Rollover Equity | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: The term “rollover equity” in M&A refers to the sale proceeds reinvested by the seller of a company into the equity of the post-acquisition company under new ownership.

sources.title: Sources and Uses of Funds | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: In short, management rollover is when the prior management team uses their equity (i.e., their stake of the pre-LBO company and exit proceeds from the sale) to help fund the transaction.

q: If an LBO's total equity requirement is $91.1 million and management rolls 10% of it, what is the management rollover amount?
explain: Management rollover is approximated as the rollover % times the total required equity: 10% x $91.1m = $9.1m; the sponsor then funds the remaining $82m.

sources.title: Sources and Uses of Funds | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: Management Rollover = 10.0% × $91.1 million = $9.1 million

sources.title: Sources and Uses of Funds | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: Sponsor Equity Contribution = $266.1 million – $184.1 million = $82 million
